opus-5.5.text:
Great question, because diversity is one of those things that's easy to talk about and surprisingly hard to measure well.

We approach it from a few angles. First, there's the distributional side: for a given prompt, we generate a large batch of images and look at how spread out they are in a learned feature space. Metrics in the spirit of recall and coverage, or pairwise distances between embeddings, tell us whether the model is exploring the space of plausible outputs or collapsing onto a handful of near-duplicates. That collapse is exactly what you often see with strong guidance or heavily fine-tuned models. They get very good at producing one "canonical" answer to a prompt.

But diversity alone isn't the goal. If you just add noise, you get diversity and garbage. So we always pair it with fidelity and alignment measures. Are the images still high quality? Do they still match the text? We look at the trade-off curve rather than a single number. The question is whether, at the same level of quality and prompt adherence, DISCO gives you a wider range of outputs. If you move along that frontier instead of just sliding along it, you've actually gained something.

Third, we look at attribute-level diversity, which is often more meaningful to people than an abstract embedding distance. For a prompt like "a person walking a dog," do you get variation in viewpoint, composition, setting, lighting, the people depicted, and the breeds of dog? Or does every sample look like the same stock photo? We can probe that with attribute classifiers or vision-language models, and see whether the distribution over those attributes is broader and more balanced.

And finally, we do human evaluation. People are quite good at noticing when a set of images feels repetitive, even when the metrics look fine. So we show raters sets of generations side by side and ask which set is more varied while still being faithful to the prompt.

No single metric tells the whole story. Embedding-based metrics can be fooled, and attribute classifiers carry their own biases. What gives us confidence is when they all point in the same direction: broader coverage, comparable quality, preserved alignment, and humans agreeing that the outputs genuinely feel more diverse.

fable-5.1.text:
Great question, because evaluating diversity turns out to be harder than evaluating quality or prompt alignment. With DISCO, we were trying to address this well-known problem that diffusion models, especially with classifier-free guidance, tend to collapse onto a handful of modes. You prompt for "a photo of a dog" and you get essentially the same golden retriever in the same pose, with slightly different backgrounds. So we needed metrics that actually capture whether we're expanding the set of plausible outputs rather than just adding noise.

We looked at it from several angles. The first is distributional: you take a fixed prompt, generate a large batch of samples, extract features with something like CLIP or DINOv2, and measure how spread out those embeddings are. We used metrics like the Vendi score and recall-oriented measures, which specifically penalize mode collapse, and we compared against the baseline model with the same prompts and same seeds. If DISCO is doing its job, you see the recall go up while precision stays roughly flat.

The second angle is semantic diversity, which is really what people care about. Spreading out in pixel space isn't meaningful if every image is still the same concept. So we used a vision-language model to tag the attributes of generated images, things like breed, color, pose, setting, and then measured the entropy over those attribute distributions. That tells us whether we're generating genuinely different dogs or just the same dog with different lighting.

The third, and I think most important, is that diversity can't come at the cost of fidelity or alignment. It's trivial to increase diversity by making the model worse. So every diversity number we report is paired with FID or a quality metric and a text-image alignment score like CLIPScore or a VQA-based measure. We plot the trade-off curves rather than reporting a single point, because that's what tells you whether the method is moving the Pareto frontier or just sliding along it.

And finally, we did human evaluation. We showed raters grids of images from the baseline and from DISCO, for the same prompt, and asked which set shows more variety while still matching the prompt. Humans are quite good at detecting when a model is just repeating itself, and that preference data aligned well with the automated metrics, which gave us confidence that we weren't optimizing for a proxy.

astra-6.text:
I would assess diversity at two levels. First, for a fixed prompt, generate multiple images and ask whether they represent meaningfully different possibilities—different compositions, appearances, and settings—not just small changes in texture or color. Second, across prompts, examine whether the model consistently favors a narrow set of representations.

For DISCO, the key comparison would be against the baseline under the same prompts, sample counts, and sampling conditions. You can use distances in a visual feature space to quantify variation, but I would pair that with human assessment and checks for image quality and prompt alignment. A model can produce more varied images simply by becoming less faithful to the prompt. What we want is broader coverage of valid interpretations while preserving quality and relevance.

sol-6.1.text:
I would look at diversity together with image quality and alignment with the prompt. You can get more variation simply by generating images that are less relevant, so diversity alone isn’t enough.

For each prompt, we would generate multiple samples and examine how much they vary—in composition, appearance, background, and other attributes the prompt leaves open. Feature-space distances can provide a quantitative signal, but I would also use human evaluation to check whether those differences are meaningful. The key comparison is whether DISCO produces a broader range of valid images than the baseline while maintaining comparable quality and text alignment.
